lessons.title: Valuing Financials: Why Price to Book and ROA Replace P/E

body.text: A bank's balance sheet is its business. Its assets are loans, its raw material is capital, and its profit depends on how hard it can work that capital without blowing up. So the right question is not 'how many times earnings am I paying?' but 'how many times book value am I paying, and does this bank earn a high enough return on that book to deserve it?'

children.text: You now understand how banks earn money and how bad loans take it away. This lesson ties it together into valuation. You will learn why P/E is a weak tool for lenders, how ROA and ROE connect through leverage, and how to work out what price to book a bank actually deserves. By the end, you will be able to explain why one bank trades below its book value while another trades at three times book, and whether either price makes sense.

columns.label: Problems with P/E for banks
points: Earnings swing with provisions, which depend on management judgement and the timing of bad loan recognition
A bank can boost this year's profit by under-providing, making the P/E look artificially low
At the bottom of a credit cycle, earnings can be near zero or negative, making P/E meaningless
P/E ignores how much capital the bank needs to generate those earnings

columns.label: Why book value works better
points: Book value is the equity capital that supports the loan book and absorbs losses
Most bank assets are financial and carried closer to realisable value than a factory's plant and machinery
Regulators set capital requirements against this equity, so it limits how fast a bank can grow
It is more stable than one year's earnings, especially through a credit cycle

children.text: ROA and ROE: Two Returns, Linked by Leverage

Return on Assets (ROA) tells you how profitably a bank uses every rupee on its balance sheet, regardless of how that balance sheet is funded. Because banks run with high leverage, a seemingly tiny ROA becomes a respectable ROE. The link is the equity multiplier: total assets divided by shareholders' equity. This is the DuPont framework applied to lenders.

body.latex: \text{ROA} = \frac{\text{Net profit}}{\text{Average total assets}} \qquad \text{ROE} = \text{ROA} \times \frac{\text{Average total assets}}{\text{Average equity}}
body.caption: ROE equals ROA multiplied by the equity multiplier (leverage)

children.text: Always check ROA alongside ROE. A bank can push ROE up simply by taking on more leverage with a thin capital base, which makes it more fragile. Two banks with the same 15% ROE are not equal if one gets there with 1.8% ROA and modest leverage, and the other with 1.0% ROA and very high leverage. As a rough guide, well-run Indian private banks have often delivered ROA in the region of 1.5% to 2%, while public sector banks spent much of the last decade well below 1% before recovering as bad loans fell.

body.title: Decompose a Bank's ROE
body.prompt: A public sector bank reports ROA of 1.1%. Its average total assets are ₹16,00,000 crore and average shareholders' equity is ₹1,00,000 crore. What is its ROE?
body.explanation: Equity multiplier = ₹16,00,000 crore ÷ ₹1,00,000 crore = 16x. ROE = 1.1% × 16 = 17.6%. That headline ROE matches a strong private bank's, but it comes from much higher leverage on a lower ROA. A modest rise in credit costs would hit this bank's equity much harder, which is one reason the market may still value it at a lower multiple of book.

children.text: What Price to Book Should a Bank Trade At?

markDefs.definition: The minimum annual return shareholders expect for the risk of owning a stock. For Indian bank stocks, analysts typically assume something in the region of 12% to 14%.

children.text: Here is the key intuition. If a bank earns exactly its

on its book value, it creates no extra value, and it should trade at about 1x book. If it earns more, each rupee of book is worth more than a rupee, so it deserves a premium. If it earns less, it destroys value on every rupee retained, and it deserves a discount. A simple formula captures this.

body.caption: Justified price to book, where g is the long-term sustainable growth rate and COE is the cost of equity. Valid only when COE is greater than g.

body.title: Justified P/B at Different ROE Levels (COE 13%, g 8%)

children.text: Notice the steep slope. At a 13% ROE, equal to the cost of equity, the bank is worth exactly book value. Every 3 percentage points of extra sustainable ROE adds 0.6x to the justified multiple in this example. This is why the market pays so much for consistently high-ROE franchises, and why a bank stuck at a 10% ROE can look 'cheap' at 0.6x book and still be overvalued.

body.title: Calculate a Justified P/B
body.prompt: A private bank is expected to earn a sustainable ROE of 17%. Its cost of equity is 13% and its long-term growth rate is 10%. What price to book multiple does the formula justify? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Justified P/B = (17% - 10%) ÷ (13% - 10%) = 7 ÷ 3 = 2.33x. Now test sensitivity: if ROE falls to 15%, it becomes 5 ÷ 3 = 1.67x, a drop of nearly 30% in fair value from a 2 percentage point fall in ROE. Bank valuations are highly sensitive to what you assume about sustainable ROE, which is why asset quality surprises move these stocks so violently.

body.title: Adjusted book value: stripping out uncovered bad loans

children.text: Reported book value assumes the loan book is worth what the balance sheet says. But net NPAs, bad loans not yet covered by provisions, may never be recovered. Analysts therefore calculate adjusted book value by subtracting net NPAs from book value, and use price to adjusted book value (P/ABV) when asset quality is a concern. Some also deduct other stressed assets or adjust for tax.

content.caption: Illustrative Bank: P/B vs P/ABV (₹ crore)

content.text: The 'discount to book' disappears once bad loans are accounted for. For banks with significant net NPAs, always compare P/ABV, not P/B.

body.title: Which Valuation Looks Hardest to Justify?
body.question: Using the illustrative peer table and assuming a cost of equity of about 13%, which bank's current P/B looks hardest to justify on its return profile alone?
body.explanation: Bank C earns an 11% ROE, below the 13% cost of equity, with weak ROA and higher GNPA than the large private banks, yet trades at 1.6x book. On returns alone it deserves a discount to book, not a premium, so the market must be pricing in a sharp improvement. Bank E also earns below its cost of equity, but its 0.5x multiple already reflects that discount. Banks A and B earn well above the cost of equity, so a premium to book is reasonable, and Bank B looks cheaper than A for a similar return profile, which is worth investigating.

body.title: Cheap Public Bank or Expensive Private Bank?
body.scenario: Your friend says: 'Why would anyone buy a large private bank at 2.8x book when you can buy a public sector bank at 0.9x book? The public bank is three times cheaper.' The private bank has delivered ROE of 16% to 18% for a decade with low GNPA. The public bank's ROE has swung between losses and 14% over the same period, and it currently reports 14%.
body.prompt: Is the public sector bank really three times cheaper? How would you evaluate the two valuations?
body.modelAnswer: Not necessarily. Price to book only means something alongside the return the bank earns on that book. The private bank has earned well above a roughly 13% cost of equity consistently, so a large premium to book can be justified: with a 17% sustainable ROE, 13% COE, and 10% growth, the formula gives about 2.3x, and investors may pay more for its consistency. The public bank's current 14% ROE would justify about 1.3x book with the same COE and growth assumptions, but the key question is whether 14% is sustainable. Its history of swinging into losses suggests the market assumes a lower through-cycle ROE, which justifies a discount. Evaluate: the average ROE across a full credit cycle, not just the latest year; ROA and leverage behind the ROE; P/ABV adjusted for net NPAs; capital adequacy and whether it may need to raise equity; and what ROE is implied by each stock's current P/B. The cheaper stock is the one whose price implies a return lower than you believe it will actually deliver.

body.text: A bank trading below book value is not automatically a bargain. If it persistently earns less than its cost of equity, every year of retained profit destroys value, and the discount can persist or widen. Many Indian public sector banks traded below book for years for exactly this reason.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: A bank that earns an ROE exactly equal to its cost of equity should, in theory, trade at a price to book of about ___ times.
body.explanation: When ROE equals the cost of equity, the bank creates no value beyond its capital, so each rupee of book value is worth about one rupee in the market.

body.title: Valuing Any Bank or NBFC
steps: Pull ROA, ROE, and book value per share for at least the last five to eight years from Screener.in or the annual reports
Calculate the equity multiplier and check whether ROE is driven by ROA or by leverage
Estimate a sustainable through-cycle ROE, not just the latest year's figure
Adjust book value for net NPAs and calculate P/ABV if asset quality is a concern
Use the justified P/B formula with a reasonable cost of equity and growth rate, and test how sensitive the answer is to ROE
Work backwards: what ROE does the current market P/B imply, and do you believe the bank can beat it?
For banks with listed subsidiaries such as insurers or AMCs, value the core bank separately from its stakes in those subsidiaries

points: P/E is a weak tool for banks because provisions distort earnings and it ignores the capital needed to generate them
ROE = ROA × equity multiplier; always check whether a high ROE comes from strong ROA or from high leverage
Justified P/B = (ROE - g) ÷ (COE - g); a bank earning its cost of equity deserves about 1x book
Bank valuations are highly sensitive to sustainable ROE, which is why asset quality surprises move bank stocks sharply
Use price to adjusted book value when net NPAs are significant
Match the valuation metric to the model: P/B for lenders, Price to Embedded Value for life insurers, P/E for asset-light AMCs and exchanges
A discount to book is only cheap if the bank can earn more than the return that discount implies

body.text: All bank figures and peer tables in this lesson are illustrative. The justified P/B formula is a simplified model and depends heavily on its assumptions. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
